Thus, four additional samples were analyzed, with four coatings from Rahn Industries: (i) BLY Gold, (ii) PSX700, (iii) P413PX, and (iv) ES-600 Gray (Figure 21). Figure 21: Samples coated with Rahn Industries coatings for corrosive environments a) BLY Gold, b) PSX700, c) P413PX, and d) ES-600 Gray The Rahn coating sample parts were immersed in the salt hydrate PCM up to the marked lines. Of the four, the preliminary inspection shows that only the BLY Gold has surface corrosion. The microscopic evaluation shows that coating degradation occurred in the BLY Gold and ES-600 Gray samples, whereas minimal degradation occurred in the PSX700 sample. The only coating that showed for degradations was the P413PX coating; therefore, it was selected as the final candidate (Figure 22). To prevent corrosion during testing, immersion coating materials were used to coat all HX surfaces. TES PCM-HX Design & Packaging To design the PCM-HX, a first-order assessment was conducted comparing several off- the-shelf HX designs for PCM storage availability, compactness, and material utilization. The PCM storage availability refers to the amount of available “free volume” where the PCM can be placed. The remaining two metrics, compactness and material utilization, are HX geometry metrics related to the HX envelope and material (tubes & fins) volumes, respectively. The first-order assessment shows that the microchannel HXs had the highest compactness and material utilization, making them an excellent design candidate for PCM-HX TES [79]. Figure 23: Comparison of PCM-HX geometries' compactness and material utilization [79] However, the challenges associated with selecting “off-the-shelf-HXs” must be addressed. Initially, header-and-serpentine microchannel HXs were the first candidates. However, both candidates (Figure 24) present their own challenges. The issue with the header MCHX is that its overall header and frame widths are 30-40% greater than the Page 29 of 127 DE-EE0009681 University of Maryland, College Park microchannel tube width. This presents a challenge when placing multiple HXs together to meet the required heat transfer surface area requirement, as the amount of PCM will increase, raising the thermal battery weight to ~1200 kg. Furthermore, this additional PCM will make only a minimal contribution to the thermal battery capacity and performance, as it will be located far from the primary heat transfer surfaces. Therefore, this weight increase defies the purpose of adjusting the thermal battery operating hours and capacity targets to meet a pre-determined constraint that the thermal battery can be no more than three times larger than the HP mass (~780 kg).
